requirement: The bundled requirements skill MUST direct agents adding or changing user-visible behavior in a Habeas project to draft stable requirement IDs and exact text, obtain the user's agreement, and install the agreed requirements in the mdBook before writing implementation or test code. It MUST direct agents to review substantive changes to agreed obligations with the user. The bootstrap skill MUST require user review of requirements inferred from existing code before installing them. The evidence skill MUST accept missing evidence or truthful false judgments from the harness while implementation is pending; it MUST NOT direct the supervising agent to write placeholder evidence itself.
rationale:
**Marking.** All three skill files are anchored with `:impl:` in `md/requirements/cli.md`. They are `assets/skills/habeas-requirements/SKILL.md`, `assets/skills/habeas-bootstrap-requirements/SKILL.md` and `assets/skills/habeas-evidence/SKILL.md`. A skill file can't carry its own reference, so a whole-file anchor is appropriate. I found no other code that implements this requirement without being marked.

**Each obligation, checked against the skill text:**
- **Draft IDs and text, obtain agreement, install before any implementation or test code.**
  - `habeas-requirements`, "New or changed behavior", tells agents to draft the smallest set of observable obligations.
  - It tells them to show the user the full IDs, the proposed chapter location and the exact fenced text.
  - It asks the user to agree or revise, and says a general request to build the feature does not count as approval.
  - It says to keep drafts out of the mdBook while review is pending and not to write implementation or test code yet.
  - Only "After agreement" does it say to install the requirements in the mdBook, confirm their names, and then implement and add tests.
- **Review substantive changes to agreed obligations with the user.**
  - `habeas-requirements` says a substantive change to an approved obligation must be reviewed and the revised requirement installed before coding that change.
  - `habeas-evidence` says to "Review a substantive change to an approved requirement with the user before changing its text."
- **Bootstrap skill requires user review of inferred requirements before installing.** `habeas-bootstrap-requirements` says requirements inferred from existing code are proposals. They are shown to the user with full IDs, exact text and uncertainty, and "Obtain agreement on the proposals before installing them in the mdBook". Prior explicit agreement to the same requirements counts.
- **Evidence skill accepts missing or truthful false evidence, and must not direct the supervising agent to write placeholder evidence.** `habeas-evidence` says "Missing evidence or a truthful false judgment is expected while implementation is pending; do not write placeholder evidence yourself." It repeatedly forbids the supervising agent from composing evidence JSON, rationales, determinations or snapshots, and from delegating that work. `habeas-requirements` adds that missing or false evidence is expected while implementation is incomplete.

**Other content.** The skills also carry guidance on directive syntax, roles and the authoring workflow. That is not user-visible program behavior. It supports the sibling skill requirements, and nothing in it contradicts this requirement.

**Tests.** No `{test}` references exist. The subject is natural-language guidance for agents, so string-matching tests would be brittle and would prove little. The text-level review above is the practical check. `tests/symposium_hook_smoke.py` and `tests/setup.rs` cover skill installation, which is a different requirement. The absence of tests is justified.

All obligations are met, so the judgment is true.

name: habeas-requirements
description: Design and vet requirements and examples for user-visible behavior changes in a Habeas mdBook project before coding; maintain definitions and references.
# Habeas requirements
## New or changed behavior

When a user requests new or changed user-visible behavior in a Habeas project, first read the relevant requirements, code, and tests. Identify requirements that already express the intended behavior. For gaps, draft the smallest set of observable obligations, including important outcomes and failure cases, without committing to an implementation.

Run `habeas info <selection>` to read current requirement and named example texts, evidence states, rationales, inputs, and validation findings as Markdown. A selection is a full name, which selects exactly, or a glob where `*` matches any number of characters, including dots, when you need to inspect a group.

Show the user the full IDs and text of existing requirements to reuse, plus the proposed chapter location, full IDs, and exact fenced text of any additions or changes. State open product choices separately. Ask the user to agree to or revise this requirement set. User-provided exact requirement text or explicit agreement earlier in the conversation counts as approval; a general request to build the feature does not. Keep drafts out of the mdBook while review is pending, and do not write implementation or test code yet.

After agreement, install the approved requirements in the mdBook and confirm their names. Then implement the behavior and add tests and traceability references. Run `habeas author --all` to create or refresh evidence through the configured model. The supervising agent must not compose evidence JSON, rationales, determinations, or source snapshots itself or delegate manual evidence writing to another agent. If implementation reveals a substantive change to an approved obligation, review and install the revised requirement before coding that change. Missing or false evidence is expected while implementation is incomplete.
## Reviewing code against requirements

The authoring harness assesses whether the code marked `{impl}` for a requirement implements every obligation completely and exactly as stated, and whether tests cover interesting design cases. It also treats as gaps any code that implements part of the requirement without `{impl}`, including code that only cites it, and any behavior in `{impl}` code that no definition implemented there specifies. When another requirement implements part of the subject, it checks only that the text carries out that part. For absent tests, it assesses whether simplicity or impracticality justifies their absence. For an example, it assesses whether test setup and assertions cover the scenario and expected outcomes. Use these criteria while implementing and fixing reported gaps; leave evidence judgments and rationales to the harness.

Requirement and example judgments have three outcomes: `true`, `false`, or `{"FIXME": ["#125"]}`. The harness uses FIXME when source comments or tests explicitly acknowledge the uncovered aspects, recording their issue references or other identifying content. A documented gap does not excuse other, unacknowledged gaps. Use the `habeas-evidence` skill for the authoring workflow.

Inspect every end-user-observable result and branch, including errors and input handling. Check that the code fulfills each applicable requirement and introduces no additional observable behavior without an agreed requirement. When requirements interact, mark every requirement implemented at the relevant point with `{impl}` and explain how their texts jointly account for the behavior. A reference alone does not explain why a behavior, such as accepting `^C`, is specified.

Every explicit function or method in first-party Rust sources needs its own requirement or example reference in an attached Rust comment or within its body, including trait methods and test helpers. A reference on an enclosing module or `impl` does not cover its functions, and there is no uncited-function waiver. If no existing requirement explains an internal helper, propose a requirement scoped to that area of internal code, such as `internal.config_parsing`, rather than one catch-all, get the user's agreement, and mark the helper with `{impl}`. That requirement's review checks that it explains each implementing function. Do not use an internal-detail requirement to justify otherwise unspecified observable behavior.
## Authoring format

Put requirements in the book's Markdown source directory. Define each with a fenced `{req}` directive: the opening line is three or more colons followed by `{req} name`, and the closing line has at least as many colons. Derive the full name from the chapter path relative to that directory: remove `.md`, change `/` to `.`, and append the directive name. For nested chapters, omit a leading `reqs/` and a trailing `/index` or `/README`.
```text
:::{req} forwarding.quit
Pressing q MUST stop managed forwards.

Everything between the fences is the requirement body, including headings and diagrams. Use a longer outer colon fence when the body contains a nested colon directive. Use BCP 14 terms when stating obligations.

Write a concrete case as a separate `{example}` directive with the same chapter-qualified naming and fence rules. Reference at least one requirement it illustrates from the example body: `{test}` when the example is a case the requirement's review should check, `{cite}` when the requirement is context for the example's own review, or both. A true example determination needs test references and an evidence rationale explaining how the tests cover its interesting aspects. Keep names unique across requirements and examples.
Use fully qualified names for implementation, citation, and test references. Place them on the relevant source or book line:
```text
{impl}`requirements.forwarding.quit`
{cite}`requirements.forwarding.quit`
{test}`requirements.forwarding.quit`
Choose the role by what the source does:

- `{impl}`: it implements part of the definition, making a decision, performing a check, producing an output, or handling a case the definition specifies. Calling code that implements the definition, or producing a result a caller uses to meet it, does not count. A requirement that refines another's obligation can `{impl}` it. A convention for every output of a kind, such as every validation error, is implemented by the code that carries it out as a whole.
- `{test}`: it is designed to verify behavior the definition specifies, through a test's scenario and assertions or an example's concrete case. Incidental setup does not count.
- `{cite}`: it relies on, supports, or refers to the definition without implementing or testing it.

`{impl}` and `{test}` make the source an input to the definition's assessment and must be covered by its evidence. `{cite}` makes the cited definition context for the citing requirement or example, needs no coverage, and does not count toward the cited requirement's implementation.

When a file that implements or tests a requirement cannot or should not carry a reference itself, such as a shipped skill, a stylesheet copied into other projects, or a README, anchor it from the declaration with `:impl: <path>` or `:test: <path>` option lines directly after the opening fence (examples accept only `:test:`). An anchor covers the whole file, so do not anchor a file when a more precise reference is available, such as a comment attached to the Rust item that implements or tests the requirement.

When a requirement or example changes, run `habeas author --all`, then the Cargo tests. Address reported implementation, test, or reference gaps and rerun the harness. Validation itself checks stored evidence without inference.
## Shared vocabulary
Use `:::{definition} name` with one nonempty `:phrase: display text` option before
its explanatory body to define shared vocabulary. Reference its chapter-qualified
name with the `{term}` role; the book renders the phrase as a plain link, without
a badge. Names are unique across requirements, examples, and definitions. A
named definition has no evidence record of its own and cannot substitute for a
requirement citation. Dependent evidence snapshots its complete declaration;
review changes to phrases and bodies because they invalidate that evidence.
name: habeas-bootstrap-requirements
description: Build an initial Habeas requirement set from an existing codebase by tracing its tests and user-visible behavior; use for requirements bootstrapping or coverage audits.
# Bootstrap requirements

Read the project's existing requirements, documentation, public entry points, implementation, and tests before writing new requirements. Follow behavior through the code rather than relying only on test names or top-level dispatch.
Keep two working inventories:
- Every first-party runnable test or test case, including integration tests, doctests, and parameterized cases where present. Record the requirement or example IDs each test checks.

- Every explicit function or method in first-party Rust sources, including trait declarations, test helpers, and internal helpers. Record its file location and the requirement or example IDs it references, with each reference's role. Also inventory relevant public APIs, commands, handlers, UI actions, configuration, outputs, errors, and distinct observable branches. Do not count one tagged entry point as coverage for deeper code.
Exclude generated and third-party code from the inventories. If a candidate looks user-facing but its purpose is unclear, keep it on the gap list until resolved.

Treat requirements inferred from existing code as proposals. Show the user their proposed full IDs and exact text, along with uncertainty about whether observed behavior is intended or a bug. Obtain agreement on the proposals before installing them in the mdBook; prior explicit agreement to the same requirements counts.

Create or reuse the agreed, stable, chapter-qualified `{req}` requirements in the mdBook. State observable obligations with BCP 14 terms. Group tests that check the same behavior under one requirement; several tests MAY share an ID. For tests of internal invariants, write a requirement for the invariant they actually check rather than inventing a user-facing promise. Distinguish intended behavior from a possible bug or incidental implementation detail.

Put at least one `{test}` reference with a full requirement or example name on each test definition or individual case, naming the definitions the test is designed to verify rather than ones it exercises incidentally. A parameterized test can carry a reference at its case source or generating declaration when that is the only editable source. Add multiple references when a test checks multiple definitions. Do not use one file-level tag to stand in for unrelated tests.

Add a requirement or example reference in a Rust comment attached to each inventoried function or method or within its body. Use `{impl}` where the function itself implements part of a definition: it makes a decision, performs a check, produces an output, or handles a case the definition specifies. Calling code that implements a definition does not count. Use `{cite}` only for code that relies on or refers to a definition without implementing or testing it; the cited requirement's review treats cite-only implementing code as a gap. An example must reference a requirement with `{test}` or `{cite}`, so an example reference still traces the function to a requirement. A reference on an enclosing module or `impl` does not cover its functions. There is no waiver for an uncited function. If no behavior-specific requirement explains an internal helper, propose an explicit requirement scoped to that area of internal code, such as `internal.config_parsing`, rather than one catch-all, get the user's agreement, and mark the helper with `{impl}`. Do not use an internal-detail requirement to justify unspecified end-user-visible behavior.

Run `habeas author --all` to create requirement and example evidence. Each assessment has its own model conversation. Each requirement's review receives the sources marked `{impl}` or `{test}` for it and can look up every source that references it, so it can find implementing code that is unmarked or only cited. It records delivered source inputs and writes judgments and rationales. The supervising agent must not compose or refresh evidence JSON, determinations, rationales, or snapshots itself, or delegate manual evidence writing to another agent. If authoring configuration or credentials are unavailable, report the blocker instead of substituting hand-written evidence.

Review every end-user-observable result and branch, including errors and input handling, when proposing requirements and adding references. Verify that the code fulfills each applicable requirement and does not introduce additional observable behavior without an agreed requirement. When requirements interact, mark each one implemented at a meaningful implementation point with `{impl}`. For example, a `^C` shortcut needs a requirement that explains why it is accepted. A tag alone does not establish that the behavior matches the requirement. Use the bundled `habeas-requirements` and `habeas-evidence` guidance for directive syntax and the authoring workflow.

The harness assesses whether the code marked `{impl}` implements each requirement completely and exactly, whether that marking is complete, with no unspecified behavior in the marked code, and whether tests cover interesting cases, allowing a rationale for absent tests when logic is simple or testing is impractical. For examples, it checks the scenario, test setup, and expected assertions; a true judgment needs a covered `{test}` reference. Its outcomes are true for supported subjects, false for unacknowledged gaps or insufficient information, and `{"FIXME": ["#125"]}` for gaps explicitly acknowledged in source comments or tests. A FIXME does not excuse additional unacknowledged gaps.
For example, source comments can carry these references:
```text
// {test}`requirements.foo`
// {impl}`requirements.foo`

After authoring, run the project tests and Habeas validation. Address reported gaps by fixing source, tests, references, or agreed requirement text, then rerun `habeas author --all` and the tests. Validation checks evidence without invoking models. Have both inventories independently reviewed against the source and tests before claiming complete coverage. Report test-tag coverage and function coverage as mapped counts over total counts. Claim 100% only when both inventories have no unmapped items and every observable branch has been reviewed. List remaining gaps with file locations and reasons; do not invent evidence or silently exclude difficult cases.
name: habeas-evidence
description: Use the Habeas authoring harness to create or refresh requirement and example evidence, and address Cargo validation failures.
# Habeas evidence
Run the authoring harness from the Cargo and mdBook project:
```sh
habeas author --all
It fills in missing, stale, or invalid evidence for requirements and named
examples. Current records are preserved, including FIXME judgments and false
judgments whose subject and inputs are unchanged; rerun one explicitly with
`habeas author <full-name>`. Each assessment runs in its own model conversation.
The harness records delivered source inputs and writes the model's judgment and
rationale. The supervising agent must not compose or refresh evidence JSON,
determinations, rationales, or source snapshots itself, or delegate that work to
an ad hoc evidence-writing agent.
Monitor summaries, outcomes, and validation diagnostics without loading generated
evidence bodies into the supervising agent's context. If a rationale needs
investigation, delegate that reading and request a concise implementation finding
rather than the evidence text.
In a Git worktree, stage new source files with `git add` before authoring.
Unstaged edits to tracked files are readable. The default exclusions are
untracked files, generated `evidence/` content, and paths outside the project;
existing Cargo build-script output directories are allowed when discoverable.
The nearest enclosing `habeas.toml` can set `[evidence]` `allow` and `disallow`
paths (literal files or directory subtrees relative to that file). Allow overrides
the defaults and disallow wins. A denied explicit read aborts that assessment;
other batch assessments continue, and the command ultimately reports failure.
The driving human or agent must decide whether to stage the file or change policy.
Do not bypass the error by writing evidence yourself.
Use `--config <name>` to select a saved authoring configuration. Configuration and
credentials can come from the user file or nearest `habeas.toml`; prefer profiles
and environment references over literal credentials in workspace files.
Bedrock defaults to concurrent assessments;
Ollama defaults to one at a time. Each named configuration's positive `concurrency`
setting overrides its default. If the provider reports throttling, lower that
setting and rerun the command. Do not substitute manual evidence creation when
configuration or provider access is missing; report the blocker.
Use `habeas status [<selection>]` to find requirements and examples needing attention,
or `--all` to include accepted records. Status groups FIXME judgments by issue;
use `--verbose` to list the judgments and original FIXME entries in each group.
Use `habeas info <selection>` to inspect their
judgments, inputs, and validation findings. A selection is a full name, which
selects exactly, or a glob matching whole names, where `*` matches any number of
characters, including dots. For a focused reassessment, run
`habeas author <full-name>`; add `--stdout` to inspect its JSON without changing
the evidence file.
Address findings by fixing implementation, tests, or source references. Review a
substantive change to an approved requirement with the user before changing its
text. Every first-party Rust function or method needs its own requirement or
example reference, including trait methods and test helpers; an enclosing module
reference does not cover its functions. Mark code `{impl}` where it implements
part of a definition and tests `{test}` where they are designed to verify it; use
`{cite}` only for related code that does neither. A requirement can `{impl}`
another requirement it refines, and an example can `{test}` or `{cite}` a
requirement. When no existing
requirement explains behavior, propose an appropriate requirement rather than
waiving the function or inventing evidence.
Missing evidence or a truthful false judgment is expected while implementation
is pending; do not write placeholder evidence yourself.
The harness assesses each requirement against the code marked `{impl}` for it
and checks that its `{test}` sources cover interesting design cases. It may
justify absent tests for simple logic or where testing is impractical. The same
review checks that the implementation is marked completely: code that implements
part of the requirement without `{impl}`, including code that only cites it, is a
gap, and so is behavior in `{impl}` code that no definition implemented there
specifies. Examples require tests covering the scenario and expected outcomes; an
accepted true judgment needs a covered `{test}` reference. `{impl}` and `{test}`
lines must be covered by the referenced definition's evidence; `{cite}` lines
need no coverage.
Requirement and example judgments are `true`, `false`, or `{"FIXME": ["#125"]}`.
FIXME means source comments or tests explicitly acknowledge every remaining gap;
the entries identify issues or other source content. The convention is
`FIXME(#125)` or `FIXME(rust-lang/rust#123)`, but other source locations are allowed.
The harness records these references; do not invent issue numbers or change a
judgment to make validation pass. CI accepts true and FIXME only when all schema,
freshness, and coverage checks also pass. Each determination stands alone: a
false judgment does not fail the definitions its subject implements, tests, or
cites.
After source or requirement fixes, rerun `habeas author --all`, then
`cargo test --workspace`. Authoring preserves completed writes when another
assessment fails, so rerunning can continue the work. A completed false judgment
still fails validation and needs its reported gaps addressed. Ordinary validation
checks stored evidence without inference; its instruction to run authoring is
for the agent, not permission for CI to call a model automatically.

Habeas MUST bundle a skill for deriving initial requirements from an existing codebase. The skill MUST direct agents to read the code and tests, map every first-party test to at least one requirement or example, identify and map every source unit implementing end-user-visible functionality or interactions to a requirement, and report gaps rather than claim complete coverage without an independent inventory review.
